metadata.narrative: Our tenant association is being asked to support a plan to tear down a deteriorated public housing development and rebuild it as a mixed-income community, possibly using RAD or a Choice Neighborhoods-style package. Residents want safer homes and better schools, but people are worried about being scattered with vouchers and never getting back. How should we judge whether this kind of redevelopment is worth supporting? What tradeoffs should we expect for current residents, children, and the surrounding neighborhood, and what protections or deal terms should we insist on before saying yes?
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: Before endorsing any redevelopment plan, the tenant association should treat "RAD" and "Choice Neighborhoods" as different tools with different built-in protections, and judge the specific deal against that distinction.

Choice Neighborhoods legislation requires grantees to offer displaced residents a right to return, one-for-one replacement of subsidized housing through new construction or vouchers, funded relocation and mobility counseling, and a linkage to local school improvement efforts.

RAD, by contrast, is fundamentally a subsidy-conversion tool letting an agency swap public housing operating subsidies for long-term project-based Section 8 contracts, and its resident protections depend on how a given deal is written rather than on a fixed statutory guarantee.

HOPE VI, the predecessor both draw from, repealed the older one-for-one replacement rule for financing flexibility, and the Urban Institute found this contributed to a near halving of deeply subsidized units nationwide, combined with return rates as low as fifty percent and poor family tracking.

That history shows the same "tear down and rebuild" label can produce very different outcomes depending on whether replacement, funded relocation support, and firm timelines are actually written into the agreement.
The track record on residents getting back into the new community is sobering and should temper optimism about "safer homes."

At Atlanta's East Lake Meadows, three-quarters of residents voted to support demolition, yet only fifteen percent ultimately returned, partly because criminal-background screening excluded entire multigenerational households over one member's record, and many struggled to find landlords willing to accept vouchers.

A scholar studying Philadelphia's Sharswood redevelopment puts the typical national return rate at only fifteen to twenty percent, and notes that mixing income levels can itself generate tension among residents rather than the hoped-for social benefits.

Chicago's Plan for Transformation research found that households relocating with vouchers, rather than into rehabbed or new mixed-income buildings, fared worse economically, landing disproportionately in high-poverty, predominantly minority neighborhoods and earning less.
That finding directly supports the fear of "being scattered and never getting back": voucher relocation is consistently the most vulnerable outcome track, not a neutral fallback.
If the proposal involves RAD-style conversion to private management, additional risks distinct from HOPE VI's history deserve scrutiny.

Tenants in New York City RAD-converted buildings have reported unremediated lead paint, mold, and substandard repairs, and moving to a private lease has meant losing legal protections while facing higher eviction rates than in traditional public housing.
Advocates elsewhere report that evictions rose after RAD conversion, some promised returnees were excluded, rents increased, and communal open space was sold to private developers.

RAD's choice-mobility feature, letting residents eventually request a voucher to move elsewhere, is also constrained because voucher demand already exceeds supply, so expanding RAD without expanding vouchers could lengthen everyone's wait.
For children, the evidence on "better schools" is more mixed than proponents suggest.

The Moving to Opportunity study found vouchers helped families reach lower-poverty, safer neighborhoods with real health gains for girls and mothers, but boys showed no benefit and sometimes worse mental health, and neither group showed consistent educational or economic gains, partly because children often kept attending the same schools regardless of address.

Children exposed to HOPE VI demolitions earned about fourteen percent more at age twenty-six than those in non-demolished projects, but researchers attributed this to improved job proximity rather than improved school quality, meaning the benefit did not necessarily come from "better schools."
This suggests the association should ask exactly how the plan intends to improve schools rather than assume redevelopment alone will do it.
On the neighborhood side, there is real quantitative evidence that safety can improve.

Urban Institute analysis of two Washington, DC HOPE VI sites found crime fell by as much as sixty percent during and after redevelopment, with reductions of about fifty percent in Milwaukee, holding even after residents moved back.

At the same time, "mixed-income" is an undefined umbrella term covering wildly different income ratios, so a plan calling itself mixed-income could still shift most units to market rate, and critics see a real risk of subsidy financing gentrification rather than serving the poorest households.
Given this record, the association should insist on specific, enforceable terms before saying yes.
First, demand a written right to return with publicly disclosed screening criteria set in advance, since vague criminal-history exclusions kept most East Lake Meadows families out.

Second, insist on one-for-one replacement of deeply subsidized units specifically, not merely "affordable" units at a higher income threshold, given how HOPE VI's abandonment of that rule nearly halved the deeply subsidized stock.

Third, if RAD conversion to a private lease is involved, push to preserve tenant rights such as the right to organize, advance notice on any action that could trigger relocation, and Enhanced Voucher rights to remain in place if a contract is not renewed.

Fourth, require funded, mandatory relocation counseling with independent, public tracking of every displaced household, since poor recordkeeping historically caused agencies to lose track of families.

Fifth, negotiate a legally enforceable Community Benefits Agreement, following models like Kingsbridge Armory's specific thirty-percent affordable-unit commitment and local living-wage hiring requirements, since a CBA is enforceable directly by the community rather than resting on unwritten promises.

Finally, get firm construction timelines with penalties for delay and guaranteed comparable off-site housing during construction, because long rebuilding schedules historically caused families to give up on returning.
Only once these terms are in writing does supporting the redevelopment become an informed decision rather than a leap of faith.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- To keep anything from a batch, call `commit_context` on that turn. It may
  appear anywhere among the turn's actions; searches in the same turn always
  run after it.
- If you issue no `commit_context` on that turn, the batch is treated as your
  decision to keep none of it: every document is dropped and the turn's other
  actions still run. That is the correct move when nothing in the batch is
  worth keeping — but it is irreversible, so do not let a batch you wanted
  lapse by forgetting.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- Issue at most one `commit_context` per turn; several are ambiguous and lose
  the batch.
- New search calls may accompany `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences) or JSON.
- Every line is a sentence of the report itself, read by someone who never saw
  this conversation. Never describe your own process: no preamble, no
  meta-commentary, no closing remarks. Lines like "Now I have committed
  evidence properly and can write the final report." or "Based on my
  research..." are not report sentences — they are shipped verbatim to the
  reader and support nothing. Start with the first real sentence of the answer.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

Choice Neighborhoods legislation requires grantees to give displaced residents the opportunity to return to redeveloped units and to provide one-for-one replacement of public or assisted housing through new construction or vouchers, plus funded relocation counseling, mobility counseling, and a defined linkage to local school improvement efforts.
The Rental Assistance Demonstration, by contrast, is fundamentally a subsidy-conversion tool that lets an agency swap public housing operating subsidies for long-term project-based Section 8 contracts, and its resident protections depend heavily on how strongly a given deal is written rather than on a fixed statutory guarantee. [shard_00135_20630]
HOPE VI, the predecessor program both draw from, repealed the older one-for-one replacement rule specifically so agencies would have more financing flexibility, and the Urban Institute found this contributed to a near halving of the number of permanently deep-subsidized units nationwide, combined with return rates as low as fifty percent and poor family tracking during relocation. [shard_05430_61229]
That history matters because it shows the same "tear down and rebuild" label can produce very different outcomes depending on whether one-for-one replacement, funded relocation support, and firm timelines are actually written into the agreement, rather than left as aspirations.

The track record on residents actually getting back into the new community is sobering and should temper optimism about "safer homes."
At Atlanta's East Lake Meadows, three-quarters of residents voted to support demolition, yet only fifteen percent of original residents ultimately returned, partly because criminal-background screening excluded entire multigenerational households over one member's record, and many families instead struggled to find landlords willing to accept vouchers. [shard_05283_74210]
A housing scholar studying Philadelphia's Sharswood redevelopment puts the typical national return rate at only fifteen to twenty percent, and notes that mixing income levels within a development can itself generate tension among residents rather than the hoped-for social benefits. [shard_00519_59464]
Chicago's Plan for Transformation research found that households who ended up relocating with vouchers rather than into rehabbed public housing or the new mixed-income buildings fared worse economically, landing disproportionately in high-poverty, predominantly minority neighborhoods, earning less, and relying more on food stamps than families in every other housing pathway examined. [shard_01847_10501]
That finding directly supports the tenant association's fear of "being scattered and never getting back": voucher relocation is consistently the most vulnerable outcome track, not a neutral fallback.

If the specific proposal on the table involves RAD-style conversion to private management, additional risks distinct from HOPE VI's history deserve scrutiny.
Tenants in New York City RAD-converted buildings have reported unremediated lead paint, toxic mold, and substandard repairs, and moving to a private lease has meant losing significant legal protections while facing higher eviction rates than in traditional public housing. [shard_05575_62493]
Advocates tracking RAD implementation elsewhere similarly report that evictions rose after conversion, some promised returnees were excluded, rents increased, and in at least one case former communal open space and recreation areas were sold to private developers. [shard_03447_31066]
The federal choice-mobility feature of RAD, which lets converted-property residents eventually request a voucher to move elsewhere, is also constrained by the fact that voucher demand already exceeds supply, so expanding RAD without expanding voucher funding could lengthen everyone's wait. [shard_01564_59031]

For children specifically, the evidence on "better schools" is more mixed than proponents often suggest.
The Moving to Opportunity study found that vouchers helped families reach lower-poverty, safer neighborhoods and produced real mental and physical health gains for girls and mothers, but boys showed no benefit and sometimes worse mental health outcomes, and neither group showed consistent educational or economic gains, partly because children often kept attending the same low-performing schools regardless of address. [shard_02063_5361]
A separate study of children exposed to HOPE VI demolitions found they earned about fourteen percent more at age twenty-six than children in non-demolished projects, but the researchers attributed this to improved proximity to jobs in the new location rather than to improved school quality or lower neighborhood poverty, meaning the benefit did not necessarily come from the "better schools" families were promised. [shard_06465_59914]
This suggests the tenant association should ask exactly how the plan intends to improve schools rather than assuming physical redevelopment alone will do it.

On the neighborhood side, there is real quantitative evidence that safety can improve.
Urban Institute analysis of two Washington, DC HOPE VI sites found crime fell by as much as sixty percent during and after redevelopment, with similar reductions of about fifty percent documented in Milwaukee, and the drops held even after original residents moved back in. [shard_01461_51824]
At the same time, researchers caution that "mixed-income" is an undefined umbrella term covering wildly different income ratios and subsidy durations, so a plan calling itself mixed-income could still shift most units to market rate, and critics see a real risk that public subsidy ends up financing gentrification rather than serving the poorest households who most need housing. [shard_06087_10598]

Given this record, the association should insist on specific, enforceable deal terms before saying yes rather than accepting general assurances.
First, demand a written, legally binding right to return with publicly disclosed screening criteria set in advance, since vague criminal-history exclusions are what kept most East Lake Meadows families out. [shard_05283_74210]
Second, insist on one-for-one replacement of deeply subsidized units specifically, not merely "affordable" units at a higher income threshold, given how HOPE VI's abandonment of that rule cut the deeply subsidized stock nearly in half. [shard_05430_61229]
Third, if RAD conversion to a private lease is part of the package, push to preserve HUD-level tenant rights such as the right to organize, advance notice and comment on any action that could trigger relocation, and Enhanced Voucher rights to remain in place at controlled rent if a contract is not renewed. [shard_02035_63433]
Fourth, require funded, mandatory relocation and mobility counseling with independent, public tracking of every displaced household, since poor recordkeeping historically caused agencies to simply lose track of families. [shard_05430_61229]
Fifth, negotiate a legally enforceable Community Benefits Agreement, following models like the Kingsbridge Armory deal's specific thirty-percent affordable-unit commitment and local living-wage hiring requirements, since a CBA is enforceable by the community coalition directly rather than depending on unwritten promises to a government agency. [shard_00652_27389] [shard_00723_50448]
Finally, get firm construction timelines with penalties for delay and guaranteed comparable off-site housing during construction, because six-year rebuilding schedules are exactly what historically caused families to give up on returning. [shard_05430_61229]
Only once these specific terms are in writing does supporting the redevelopment become a reasonably informed decision rather than a leap of faith.
